current_answer: A new theory says AI can change hiring before anyone is hired: if AI-assisted applications make written materials less informative, employers may put more weight on prior experience and screen fewer inexperienced candidates. The paper does not test this with real applicants or employers. Measured U.S. evidence still shows a narrower, unresolved entry-route warning: highly AI-exposed work can have fewer junior openings even when advertised pay rises. Those exposure-based results do not prove AI caused the pattern. Yale’s broad U.S. monitor still finds no clear economy-wide footprint. The live conclusion is not mass unemployment; it is that entry routes may be changing through several possible channels that need direct measurement.

catalogue_card.question: Could AI make it harder to prove you are the right candidate?
catalogue_card.text: A new hiring model says AI-written applications could make employers lean harder on prior experience. It is a theory, not evidence that real employers are screening fewer people.

summary: A new formal model asks what happens when AI makes applications easier to generate and tailor but less useful as evidence of applicant fit. It predicts that employers may rely more on prior experience when screening is costly.

In the model, inexperienced applicants who are a good fit can lose screening opportunities because their written materials no longer distinguish them as well. A lower-cost intermediate assessment can restore a path to screening.
This is not hiring data. The paper does not observe AI-assisted applications, employers, interviews, offers, hires, wages, employment or layoffs.

Measured U.S. posting and graduate evidence still supports only a narrower, exposure-based concern about entry routes. A broad U.S. monitor still finds no clear economy-wide AI labor-market footprint.
uncertainty: The new paper is a theoretical preprint. It does not measure application assistance, screening, interviews, offers, hires, wages, employment or layoffs.
The U.S. junior-opening and early-career results use occupational exposure rather than records of employer AI deployment, so their causal attribution remains unresolved.
A broad U.S. monitor, regional postings, graduate records and theory cover different populations and outcomes. Together they do not establish a national effect or a personal forecast.
freshness_note: Checked 26 September 2026. A new theoretical hiring paper adds a plausible screening channel for entry barriers, but it is not empirical evidence of changed hiring or an economy-wide labor-market effect.
